You're likely referring to the Russian Tsar Nicholas II, not one from the 1700s. The Russian Tsar Nicholas II, along with his wife Alexandra and their children, was executed by the Bolsheviks in 1918. 

The last Russian Tsar, Nicholas II, was a member of the Romanov dynasty, which had ruled Russia for over 300 years. However, his reign was marked by a series of challenges, including a devastating war and economic troubles. The family was overthrown in the February Revolution in 1917 and subsequently exiled to Tobolsk.

After the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, took control of Russia. Nicholas II, his wife Alexandra, and their children were eventually moved to Yekaterinburg, where they were under house arrest.

On July 17, 1918, a group of Bolsheviks, led by Yakov Yurovsky, executed the Russian royal family in a basement room of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg. The family, including Nicholas II, Alexandra, their four daughters, and their son, as well as four loyal servants, were brutally shot. The bodies were later buried in a secret grave and later relocated to the St. Catherine Chapel at the St. Peter and St. Paul Cathedral in St. Petersburg (now Leningrad).

The news of the execution was initially kept secret, but it eventually became public knowledge, and it contributed to the widespread outrage and anger among Russians against the Bolsheviks.

So, to summarize, the Russian Tsar Nicholas II and his family were executed by the Bolsheviks in 1918, marking the end of the Romanov dynasty.

The Russian Tsar in the 1700s you might be referring to is Peter the Great, who reigned from 1682 until his death in 1725. Peter the Great was a significant figure in Russian history, known for his extensive reforms aimed at modernizing Russia and making it a major European power. He moved the capital from Moscow to Saint Petersburg, which he founded in 1703, and he greatly expanded the Russian Empire.

As for his family, Peter the Great had several children, but his relationship with his son, Tsarevich Alexei Petrovich, was particularly tumultuous. Alexei was Peter's son from his first marriage to Eudoxia Lopukhina. Peter and Alexei had a strained relationship, largely due to their differing views on Russia's future. Alexei was more conservative and opposed his father's Westernizing reforms.

In 1718, Alexei was accused of conspiring against his father. He was arrested, tortured, and forced to name his co-conspirators. After a trial, Alexei was sentenced to death, but he died in prison before the sentence could be carried out, possibly due to the effects of torture.

Peter the Great's second wife, Catherine I, succeeded him as Empress of Russia after his death in 1725. She was the first woman to rule Imperial Russia, opening the door for future female rulers like Empress Elizabeth and Catherine the Great.

The period following Peter the Great's death was marked by political instability, with several short-lived rulers and power struggles among the nobility. This era, known as the Time of Troubles, ended with the ascension of the Romanov dynasty, which would rule Russia until the Russian Revolution of 1917.

The Russian Tsar you're likely referring to is Tsar Peter III, who reigned between 1762 and 1763. His reign was extremely short as he was deposed and murdered just eight months after ascending the throne.

Peter III ascended to the throne upon the death of his mother, Empress Elizabeth, who had no surviving children. He was not particularly popular, as he was a pro-Prussian sympathizer in a nation that was more pro-Austrian. Additionally, he announced his intention to abdicate in favor of a Hessian prince, which caused dissatisfaction among the Russian nobility.

A coup led by his wife, Catherine the Great, and other key figures deposed Peter III and placed Catherine on the throne. Peter was imprisoned and eventually murdered, although the exact circumstances of his death are not definitively known. He was succeeded by his wife Catherine, who became one of the most powerful and influential rulers in Russian history.

The Russian Tsar you're likely referring to is Tsar Peter III (reigned from 1762 until his death in 1762). He ascended to the throne following the death of his father, Emperor Peter the Great, and was overthrown after only six months by his wife, Catherine II (later known as Catherine the Great), with the support of his own guards.

Peter III was known for his pro-Prussian policies, which were unpopular among the Russian nobility. His brief reign was marked by several unpopular decisions, including his attempt to dissolve the Preobrazhensky and Semenovsky Guards, and his pro-Prussian orientation.

On the night of July 8–9, 1762, Catherine organized a coup d'état, with the support of her close confidants and the Preobrazhensky and Semenovsky Guards. Peter III was taken from the palace and imprisoned in Ropsha, where he died mysteriously three days later, leading to speculation that he was poisoned on Catherine's orders. After Peter's death, Catherine was proclaimed Empress by the Preobrazhensky and Semenovsky Guard, marking the beginning of her 34-year reign.

As for Peter III's family, his oldest son, Grand Duke Paul, was a minor at the time and was taken into Catherine's care. He later became emperor in 1796 upon Catherine's death. Peter's other son, Grand Duke Alexei, was kept under house arrest and died under suspicious circumstances in 1780. Peter's daughter, Grand Duchess Anna, was also placed under house arrest after her mother's accession and died in 1776.
